title: Plain language: Writing for understanding (digital.gov, ex plainlanguage.gov)
topic: active voice, present tense, hidden verbs
rule: Name the actor (active voice); prefer present tense; turn hidden verbs (-ment/-tion/-ance nouns after weak verbs make/take/give/have) back into verbs; short words and short sections; address the reader as 'you' and name the actor as 'we'. Passive is acceptable when the only actor is the law itself.
example: 'We make a decision on each claim' -> 'We decide each claim'; 'Applicants who submitted late will be charged a fee' -> 'Applicants who submit late pay a fee'
llm_tell: Models write about twice the human rate of nominalisations; this rule is the direct counter and is consistent with the existing 'People do things' rule.

title: Plain language guide index (plainlanguage.gov moved here)
rule: Plain language is content written for its specific audience; the US Plain Writing Act of 2010 requires it for public content. The guide has four parts: principles, writing, design, testing. Testing with the audience is part of the standard, not an extra. Old guidelines are archived in the GSA PlainLanguage.gov GitHub repo (_pages/guidelines), not read here.

title: Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities (W3C COGA)
rule: Use clear literal language; avoid metaphor, idiom and non-literal text, which people with social or communication disabilities may not understand. Do not rely on tone, joke or image to carry meaning: say the implied thing in text. Use familiar vocabulary, short sentences and short blocks, and offer a short summary of long content. Summarizer read only the first ~100k of 470k characters and said section 4 patterns were cut off, so patterns in 4.4 (language) and 4.5 (errors) are unread; the examples below are the fetch model's own illustrations, not W3C text.
example: Fetch-model illustration, not W3C: 'Hit the ground running with our new plan' -> 'Start using the new plan today'
llm_tell: Figurative flourish and aphoristic closers are the shared LLM fiction tell; here the same device is a documented access barrier.

title: W3C COGA: instructions, errors and numbers
rule: Give clear labels, step-by-step instructions and specific error messages that say exactly what to do. Explain unusual controls and their consequences in plain words. People with numerical-comprehension difficulty may confuse percentages and numeric references; give a words alternative to numbers where possible. Include the accents and diacritics needed for speech synthesis to read words correctly. COGA names these needs; the 'avoid/use' error-message text was not read.
example: Fetch-model illustration, not W3C: 'Invalid input' -> 'Enter a date in this format: DD/MM/YYYY, for example 05/04/2024'

title: Understanding SC 3.1.5 Reading Level (WCAG 2.1, Level AAA)
rule: When text needs more than lower-secondary reading ability (about school years 7 to 9), after setting aside proper names and titles, provide supplemental content or a version that does not need it. No formula or score is prescribed: education level can be judged by qualified teachers against local standards. Sufficient techniques: plain summary (G86), illustrations (G103), spoken version (G79), easier text (G153), sign language (G160). Multilingual pages are judged per language (each language of at least 5% of content in full sentences), by the worst result. It is Level AAA, so aspirational, not a conformance requirement.

title: Understanding SC 1.4.1 Use of Color (WCAG 2.1, Level A)
rule: Colour must not be the only means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response or distinguishing an element. Pair it with text, shape, icon or pattern. Failures: required or error fields marked only by colour (F81), links distinguishable only by colour (F73), image alt text that omits what colour conveys (F13). If meaning depends on a specific colour (green valid, red invalid), an extra indicator is still required even with 3:1 lightness contrast. Directly limits a game-voice rule that lets direction ride on colour.
example: 'Required fields are red' -> add 'required' text or an icon to the label

title: WebAIM: Alternative Text
rule: Every img has an alt attribute; decorative images get alt="" (test: if removed, is meaning lost? no -> empty). Keep it to a few words; a sentence or two is rarely needed. Do not write 'image of' or 'graphic of'; do not repeat nearby text or the figcaption. For linked or button images describe the function or destination, not the picture ('Search', 'PDF'); an image that is the only content of a link must not have empty alt. Logo: company name, no 'logo'. Charts and maps: a short phrase for what it is, with the full detail in an adjacent table or body text. Content-bearing images belong in markup, not CSS.
example: Linked photo with no other link text: alt="Astronaut Ellen Ochoa"
llm_tell: Not read for tells. Models tend to write long descriptive alt text opening 'An image of...'; that is my inference, unmeasured.

title: Readability formulas, programs and tools: Do they work for plain language? (Government of Canada) via search snippets
rule: Per search-result summaries only (page itself returned 403 on fetch): Kern (1980) is reported to have found that formulas cannot match material to readers at a target grade and that rewriting to lower the grade score does not raise comprehension; writers can learn to game the score. Redish: most of what makes a document usable is not in the formulas. Formulas assume short words are always easier, but familiarity to the audience is what matters. They ignore organisation, formatting and page density. Counterpoint (Michigan Bar Journal, via snippet): Flesch and Kincaid were built and tested on adults and are reasonably, not perfectly, reliable as a coarse first screen. Kern and Redish originals not read.
llm_tell: A readability score is a proxy a model can hit while the text stays unclear; use it only as a screen. Consistent with the skill's rule against regex gates on prose.

title: Information for all: European easy-to-read standards (Inclusion Europe)
rule: Per snippets only; the detailed rules are in a PDF that was not read. Use plain vocabulary, explain unavoidable hard terms, and use the same word for the same thing throughout (example given: 'End' not 'Terminate'). Texts should be reviewed by people with intellectual disabilities; that review is described as the one requirement that separates real easy-to-read from merely simplified text ('Do not write for us without us'). Whether Easy Read counts as a version of the page or a replacement for it was not established.
llm_tell: Elegant variation (rotating synonyms for one thing) is a known model habit and is the opposite of this rule.

title: Global English / writing for non-native readers (search-result summaries: Home Office, Microsoft, Document360, SAS, Techscribe)
rule: Per snippets only. Replace idioms, slang and culture-bound phrases ('circle back') with literal wording. Replace phrasal verbs ('look up', 'carry out') with single verbs, because many have several meanings. For machine translation keep sentences under about 25 words, avoid sentence fragments, and avoid chaining clauses with 'which' or 'although'; limit noun stacks to about three words. Tension: one critique (Techscribe) says native-speaker plain English advice, such as short verbs and cutting words, conflicts with global-English advice. The UK Home Office page moved and was not read; the Document360 and SAS figures are vendor-blog advice, not studies.
llm_tell: Models produce idiom and phrasal verbs freely ('dive into', 'unlock', 'navigate'); this is the plain-language reason to cut them as well as the stylistic one.

title: Where plain-language rules conflict with game voice and stylish rules
rule: My own reading of the sources, not a source's claim. (1) Figurative language, aphorism and wry understatement, which this skill treats as human craft in fiction, are access barriers under COGA. (2) 'Leave the last step to the reader' is wrong for instructions, errors and safety text, where COGA says to state the implied thing. (3) 'Direction can ride on colour' fails WCAG 1.4.1. (4) Terse effect lines and non-explained mechanics need a literal fallback (a tooltip or help line) if the game is to be readable at 3.1.5. (5) Same-word-for-same-thing contradicts the elegant variation good prose uses. (6) Short-word advice is not universal: choose words familiar to the audience, which is the formula critique. Resolution needs a decision per venue; not tested with readers.
